cards.front: Why are capacitors called the opposite of inductors?
cards.back: Almost every behaviour is reversed: Xc falls with frequency (Xl rises), current leads (Xl lags), Xc → ∞ at DC (Xl → 0).

cards.front: Can current flow THROUGH a capacitor?
cards.back: No electrons cross the dielectric. But on AC, current flows continuously in the circuit as the capacitor charges, discharges and recharges — it "appears" to flow through.

cards.front: Explain the two-tank analogy.
cards.back: A reversing pump moves water back and forth between two tanks: flow never stops, but no water passes directly from tank to tank. Same as electrons charging each plate in turn.

cards.front: Why does current "appear to flow" through a capacitor?
cards.back: Because the AC voltage continuously rises, falls and reverses, keeping the capacitor charging and discharging.

cards.front: Does a capacitor block AC or DC?
cards.back: It blocks steady DC (after charging) and passes AC — more easily at higher frequency.

cards.front: What is the impressed voltage?
cards.back: The voltage built up across the plates by the stored charge. It opposes the applied voltage and limits current.

cards.front: Phase relationship of impressed and applied voltage?
cards.back: 180° apart.

cards.front: What is capacitive reactance?
cards.back: The current-limiting effect of a capacitor (its countervoltage), symbol Xc, measured in ohms.

cards.front: Formula for Xc?
cards.back: Xc = 1 / (2πfC)  (f in Hz, C in farads)

cards.front: Rearranged Xc formulas?
cards.back: C = 1 / (2πf·Xc) and f = 1 / (2πC·Xc)

cards.front: Two factors that determine capacitive reactance?
cards.back: Capacitance and frequency — Xc is INVERSELY proportional to both.

cards.front: 35 µF on 120 V, 60 Hz: Xc and current?
480 V, 60 Hz, 2.6 A: capacitance?
Most common Xc calculation error?
cards.back: Leaving C in µF instead of converting to farads (35 µF = 0.000035 F). Also forgetting the reciprocal (1/x).

cards.front: Xc of a capacitor at DC?
cards.back: Infinite — it blocks steady DC (opposite of an inductor, whose Xl = 0 at DC).

cards.front: Frequency doubles. What happens to Xc and current?
cards.back: Xc halves; current doubles.

cards.front: Why does Xc drop as frequency rises?
cards.back: Current is charge per second (I = Q/t). At higher frequency the same charge moves in less time, so more current flows for the same voltage.

cards.front: 300 Ω at 60 Hz. Xc at 100 Hz?
Book table error check: 470 nF at 400 Hz?
cards.back: 846.6 Ω (the book's Table 20–1 says kΩ). Also 470 nF @ 1 kHz = 338.6 Ω and 750 nF @ 400 Hz = 530.5 Ω.

cards.front: Phase of current vs voltage in a pure capacitive circuit?
cards.back: Current LEADS the applied voltage by 90°.

cards.front: What does "ELI the ICE man" say about capacitors?
cards.back: ICE: in a capacitor (C), current (I) comes before voltage (E).

cards.front: Why is capacitor current maximum when voltage is zero?
cards.back: Current depends on how fast the charge changes. At 0° the voltage (and charge) is changing fastest; at 90° it's at peak and momentarily not changing, so current = 0.

cards.front: Compare phase in R, L and C circuits.
cards.back: R: in phase. L: current lags 90°. C: current leads 90°.

cards.front: Charge on a capacitor vs applied voltage?
cards.back: In phase: Q = C × V, so charge is zero when voltage is zero and peaks when voltage peaks.

cards.front: True power in a pure capacitive circuit?
cards.back: Zero watts — energy stored while charging is returned while discharging.

cards.front: What do the gold and red areas represent?
cards.back: Gold: V and I same sign — charging, storing energy in the electrostatic field. Red: opposite signs — discharging, returning energy.

cards.front: Why does P = E × I × cos θ give zero for a pure capacitor?
cards.back: θ = 90° and cos 90° = 0.

cards.front: What unit is capacitor power measured in?
cards.back: VARs (volt-amperes-reactive), written VARsC.

cards.front: Formulas for VARsC?
cards.back: VARsC = Ec × Ic = Ic² × Xc = Ec² / Xc

cards.front: How are capacitive and inductive VARs related?
cards.back: 180° out of phase — they cancel each other.

cards.front: Why do plants install capacitor banks rated in kVAR?
cards.back: Their leading (capacitive) VARs cancel the motors' lagging (inductive) VARs, so the utility supplies less current and PF improves.

cards.front: Q of a capacitor: formula?
cards.back: Q = R / Xc, where R is the dielectric's (leakage) resistance.
cards.note: Flipped from an inductor's Q = Xl/R

cards.front: Other Q formulas for a capacitor?
cards.back: Q = VARsC / P, and approximately Q ≈ 1/PF (accurate when Q is high).

cards.front: Is a capacitor's Q usually high or low? What lowers it?
cards.back: Very high. A leaky dielectric (lower R) lowers Q.

cards.front: What is a capacitor's voltage rating really the rating of?
cards.back: The dielectric.

cards.front: A nonpolarized capacitor is marked in VAC. What value is that?
cards.back: RMS — compare directly with the circuit's RMS voltage.

cards.front: Marked VDC, WVDC or PEAK. How do you use it on AC?
cards.back: It's a PEAK value: compare it with the circuit's RMS × 1.414.

cards.front: How are electrolytic (polarized) capacitors rated?
cards.back: Always in DC volts.

cards.front: 300 WVDC capacitor on a 240 V line. OK?
cards.back: No: 240 × 1.414 = 339 V peak, which exceeds 300 V.

cards.front: 600 VDC capacitor on 480 VAC. OK?
A 350 VAC capacitor is equivalent to what DC rating?
cards.back: About 350 × 1.414 ≈ 495 V peak (DC).

cards.front: Life gain at half the rated voltage?
cards.back: About 8×.

cards.front: Is there a standard for how capacitor voltage ratings are marked?
cards.back: No — you'll see VOLTS AC, VOLTS DC, PEAK VOLTS and WVDC. Read the label carefully.

cards.front: In series, how do capacitive REACTANCES combine?
cards.back: They add: Xct = Xc1 + Xc2 + Xc3 (same angle).

cards.front: In parallel, how do capacitive REACTANCES combine?
cards.back: Reciprocal formula: 1/Xct = 1/Xc1 + 1/Xc2 + 1/Xc3.

cards.front: 10, 30, 15 µF in series on 480 V, 60 Hz. Xct, Ct and I?
In that series circuit, which capacitor has the largest voltage drop?
cards.back: The smallest one (10 µF): 240 V. Drops are 240, 80, 160 V.

cards.front: Do the series capacitor voltage drops add straight?
cards.back: Yes — all capacitor drops are in phase with each other (240 + 80 + 160 = 480 V).

cards.front: 50, 75, 20 µF in parallel, 787 VARs at 60 Hz. Find E.
Formula for E from VARs and reactance?
cards.back: E = √(VARs × X)

cards.front: Do VARs from several capacitors add?
cards.back: Yes — same-type VARs add straight in series or parallel.

cards.front: Capacitor drawn onto a higher voltage than rated: two effects?
cards.back: VARs rise with V² (480 → 600 V ≈ +56% kVAR) and the dielectric is overstressed.

cards.front: Why can PF capacitors overheat on VFD/electronic systems?
cards.back: Their Xc drops at harmonic frequencies, so they draw extra harmonic current and can resonate with system inductance.

cards.front: Field formula to check a run capacitor at 60 Hz?
cards.back: C (µF) ≈ 2652 × I ÷ E (current through it, voltage across it).

cards.front: Add a series capacitor to reduce current from 24 A to 16 A on 480 V. Method?
cards.back: Existing Xc = 480/24; needed total = 480/16; series Xc's add, so the new cap supplies the difference in Xc. Convert that Xc to µF.

cards.front: Four equal capacitors in series must total 20 µF. Value of each?
cards.back: C/N = 20 µF → each = 80 µF; each sees ¼ of the line voltage.
